nodes.label: Driver
nodes.summary: Sends GPS location every few seconds. Noisy fixes are cleaned by map matching.
nodes.details: A 2015 talk (via a secondary summary, not re-verified) put the interval at about 4 s.

nodes.label: Rider
nodes.summary: Requests a ride at a pickup point and receives a match.

nodes.label: Location ingestion
nodes.summary: Receives driver pings, map-matches them to road segments and writes the latest position. The write path dominates traffic.

nodes.label: H3 cell index
nodes.summary: Turns (lat, lng) into a 64-bit hexagonal cell ID at a chosen resolution. Nearby search = the cell plus its k-ring of neighbours (grid_disk). 16 resolutions. Parent cell = bit truncation.
nodes.details: Res 9 ≈ 0.105 km² per cell, res 8 ≈ 0.737 km². Hexagons have one distance to every neighbour. Uber built H3 for pricing and dispatch.

nodes.label: In-memory geo index (sharded by cell)
nodes.summary: Holds the latest drivers per cell. A query looks up the rider's cell and its neighbouring cells, then filters by distance and availability.
nodes.details: In a 2015 description (secondary source, not re-verified) the shard key was a Google S2 level-12 cell and nodes formed a Ringpop ring. H3 came in 2018.

nodes.label: Latest-location cache (Redis)
nodes.summary: Latest position and a short buffer per driver. Fast reads for matching.

nodes.label: Location history (Cassandra)
nodes.summary: Durable, write-heavy history for analytics and replay.

nodes.label: Matching / dispatch
nodes.summary: Waits a few seconds, collects nearby riders and drivers into a batch and chooses pairings to reduce average wait for everyone, not just the closest pair.
nodes.details: Uber says early matching picked the closest driver immediately and that closest does not always mean quickest. Whether the batch is solved as an assignment problem is our interpretation.

nodes.label: ETA service
nodes.summary: Ranks candidates by estimated arrival time over the road network instead of straight-line distance.
nodes.details: The Uber matching page we read does not describe ETA computation.

nodes.label: Pricing by hexagon
nodes.summary: Supply and demand are measured per H3 hexagon in each city to calculate surge.

steps.caption: The driver app sends its location every few seconds.
The index converts the cleaned position into an H3 cell ID, a single 64-bit integer, at the chosen resolution.
The driver is moved from their old cell to the new one in the in-memory index, sharded by cell.
The latest position is also cached for fast reads.
History is appended asynchronously to durable storage.
The rider's request reaches matching. Uber evaluates nearby drivers and riders in one batch over a few seconds instead of taking the closest driver immediately.
The pickup becomes a cell plus a ring of neighbouring cells. Hexagons make all neighbours equidistant, so the search area grows evenly.
Matching reads the drivers in those cells: key lookups, not a 2-D distance scan.
Candidates are ranked by estimated arrival time, not straight-line distance.
The chosen driver receives the offer.
Supply and demand are counted per H3 hexagon. Uber says it calculates surge by measuring them in hexagons in each city.
A burst of requests maps to the same few cells.
Those cell shards take the most reads. Finer H3 resolutions and splitting hot shards spread the load (our design reasoning).
Candidates are still ranked by arrival time before an offer is made.
